Christmas Eve, at the trattoria "Da Graziella". It's exactly a year since Matei proposed to Giulia on Ponte Santa Trinita. Professor Bellini comes in with a parcel wrapped in brown paper.
Good evening and happy Christmas. Sorry I'm late: for the first time in my life, I've arrived after the agreed time.
Professor! Do sit down. And that parcel?
It's for Matei and Giulia. It's my grandfather Ernesto's diary. He wrote it during the flood of 1966.
Ernesto's diary? Professor, we can't accept it.
You can and you must. I have no children. And in my opinion a diary should stay in the hands of those who understand it.
Will you read us the beginning, Professor?

(reads) "On the 4th of November 1966 the Arno burst its banks. The water reached Santa Croce at seven in the morning. I ran towards the workshop, but I could not get in. The mud was already a metre deep."
Burst, reached, ran… He talks like a school textbook!
It's the passato remoto. My grandfather was a nineteenth-century man: for him, every day was already history.
You'll find that out for yourselves. I'll just tell you that on page forty there's a name you know. And the last page talks about a very small brush.
Exactly. And now, Signora Graziella, if you don't bring me a plate of tortellini in broth right away, I'll be using the passato remoto to describe how I died of hunger.

1. What the passato remoto is and where you'll meet it

The passato remoto ("remote past") is the tense of novels, fairy tales, biographies and history books. It's like the simple past of literary English ("he came, he saw, he conquered"). At A2 you only need to RECOGNISE it when you read.
Once upon a time there was a king who had three daughters.
Dante was born in Florence in 1265.
In Southern Italy (Naples, Sicily) the passato remoto is also used in everyday speech: Assunta might say "Ieri andai al mercato." In the North, hardly at all.
In stories you'll mostly meet the 3rd person (lui / lei, loro). Learn to recognise them by their endings:
Watch the accent: "arrivò" (he arrived) ≠ "arrivo" (I arrive). "parlò" (he spoke) ≠ "parlo" (I speak). The written accent changes everything!
Trick: many irregular forms have "-ss-" (disse, scrisse) or are one short syllable (fu, mise, vide). If you see an unknown verb ending in "-e" with a past meaning, it may be a passato remoto.
Nel 1966 Ernesto vide l’Arno uscire dal letto.
When you speak, use the passato prossimo. You'll practise the passato remoto actively at B1–B2. For now, you recognise and understand it.
La torta è stata preparata. Si balla.
Siccome… / da due anni / dopo aver…
Se è una bambina… Avrei voluto…

That Christmas, for the first time, both of Giulia's families got together in Florence. Rosaria and Gennaro came from Naples with six trays of struffoli. With them came Grandma Assunta, who at ninety-two had never been to Florence. As soon as she got off the train, she looked at the dome of the Duomo and said: "Pretty. But Vesuvius is bigger."

On Christmas night, after midnight Mass at Santo Spirito, they all stayed on in the trattoria, around the nativity scene that Grandpa Renzo, Graziella's father, had built many years before, and which Graziella brought out every December. Matei opened Ernesto's diary on the table. It was a black notebook, with yellowed pages and a dark stain on the cover: mud from 1966, still there after sixty years.

Giulia began to read aloud. Ernesto wrote well, in short sentences, like a man who doesn't want to waste time. "On the 4th of November the water entered the workshop and destroyed everything that was on the floor. The next day I went back with two assistants. We found the paintings under a metre of mud. I wept, but only a little, because there was no time."

"On the 6th of November the first young people arrived. They came from all over Italy and all over the world: students, workers, even foreigners who did not speak a word of Italian. They were called 'mud angels'. They carried buckets, worked twelve hours a day, slept wherever they could. They never asked for anything."

Then Giulia reached page forty. She read the first line, stopped and looked at Graziella. "Read it," said Graziella, who didn't understand. Giulia went on, slowly: "On the 12th of November a young man from Bologna came looking for me. He was tall, very thin, with a red bicycle covered in mud. He said his name was Aldo and that he wanted to help. I gave him a bucket and a pair of boots."

In the trattoria you couldn't hear a thing, not even the fire in the hearth. Graziella raised a hand to her mouth. Giulia went on. "On the 15th of November Aldo and I went into the church of San Frediano. The Madonna was still on the altar, but the water had reached the Virgin's feet. Together we took her down from the wall. She weighed as much as a man. Aldo carried her out on his shoulders, in the rain, and did not let her fall."

"It's him," Graziella whispered. "It's my Aldo. He'd told me about the flood, the mud, the bicycle. But he never said anything about a Madonna. Never. In forty years." She took the diary from Giulia's hands and touched the page with her fingers, the way you touch a photograph. "That's how he was. He did beautiful things and then forgot all about them."

Matei looked at Bellini. "Professor, did you know?" Bellini nodded. "I read it for the first time three months ago, after your wedding. I couldn't believe it. The Madonna you found in Sibiu, the one with my grandfather's letter behind it, is the same one Aldo carried out on his shoulders. Sometimes fate has a sense of humour that not even Caravaggio could have imagined."

There was still the last page. This time Matei read it. "On the 20th of December Aldo went back to Bologna. Before leaving he asked me for a keepsake. I gave him my biggest brush, the one I used for skies. The smallest I am keeping for my grandson, who is just two years old. One day I will tell him: 'Look. And don't touch anything.' When he is grown up, he will understand that it is the most important rule of our profession. And of life."

Graziella got up without saying anything and went upstairs. She came back five minutes later with something wrapped in an old handkerchief. She opened it on the table. Inside was a wide brush, with a worn handle and bristles that were still a little blue. "It was in one of Aldo's drawers," she said. "I've kept it for ten years without knowing why. Now I know."

Bellini placed beside it Ernesto's small brush, which Matei had brought down from the shelf. The big one and the small one. The sky and the details. They all stayed there looking at them in silence, at half past midnight, among Rosaria's struffoli and Grandpa Renzo's nativity scene. Assunta, who hadn't understood everything but had understood what mattered, crossed herself.

Then Giulia felt something. A little movement, like a butterfly, under the hand she was resting on her stomach. The first. She took Matei's hand and placed it on the same spot. They waited. And the baby, as if it had listened to the whole story, moved again. "Happy Christmas," Matei said softly to the bump. And it was the most beautiful Christmas anyone in that trattoria could remember.
